repository.description: Turn conda-forge, Spack, and EasyBuild recipes into Resolvo-solved variants, CycloneDX SBOMs, and build-evaluated package bundles
repository.name: eb-stack
repository.readme:
**Turn foreign and EasyBuild recipes into resolved, build-evaluated package bundles.** `eb-stack` parses conda-forge, Spack, PyPI, Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN), Cargo, LuaRocks, Raku, and EasyBuild recipes into one canonical package plan. It emits a planned CycloneDX Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), solves each product profile with Resolvo, writes one conventional `.eb` file per installable variant, and drives the recipes through a persisted remote build campaign. A plan is not a build. `package plan` and `package bump` can establish only **resolves**. `campaign run` owns **builds** and **binary-verified**. The GitHub release and the crates.io package are 0.7.4 and carry every command here. The [glossary](docs/orgmode/reference/glossary.org) defines closure, generation, baseline, and reachability. The longer path is the [tutorial](docs/orgmode/tutorial.org). [![CI](https://github.com/stackhands/eb-stack/actions/workflows/ci_test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/stackhands/eb-stack/actions/workflows/ci_test.yml) [![Docs](https://github.com/stackhands/eb-stack/actions/workflows/ci_docs.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/stackhands/eb-stack/actions/workflows/ci_docs.yml) [![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/eb_stack.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/eb_stack) [![docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-eb--stack.rgoswami.me-blue)](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE) ## Discovery - [llms.txt](llms.txt) indexes the manual. [llms-full.txt](llms-full.txt) repeats every page in one file. - [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) describes contribution and validation requirements. - The skills for inspect, plan, bump, a stack SBOM, pull-request overlap, and the stdio server are under [skills/](skills/). - The Model Context Protocol manifest is [server.json](server.json). Client configuration is the manual page [Model Context Protocol server](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/reference/mcp.html). ## Pipeline

```text conda-forge / Spack / EasyBuild │ ▼ canonical package.plan.json ─── package.sbom.cdx.json │ ▼ profile materialization + stack policy + Resolvo │ ├── locks/.lock.json └── easyconfigs///.eb │ ▼ target-routed campaign + typed findings ``` New packages and bumps use the same artifacts. A bump is an EasyBuild-origin plan plus SBOM and Resolvo lock, not a standalone text rewrite. ## Claim ladder

Report these claims independently: 1. **resolves**: every requested profile has a Resolvo lock and emitted recipe; 2. **builds**: every emitted recipe completes through EasyBuild on the configured target; 3. **binary-verified**: every declared profile verification command succeeds. `package inspect` establishes none of them. `package plan` and `package bump` can establish only `resolves`. `campaign run` owns the other two. ## Install The crate is `eb_stack` on crates.io; the installed binary is `eb-stack`. Rust 1.90 or newer is required when building from source. `rustc` 1.83 stops while reading the crate index: the Cargo feature `edition2024` is not stabilized. `rustup toolchain install stable` and `rustup default stable` provide a new enough compiler. The GitHub release is 0.7.4, with installers and archives for Linux (x86-64, aarch64), macOS and Windows, and `eb-stack --version` prints `0.7.4` for it, as a build of this tree does. `cargo install eb_stack --locked` builds the same 0.7.4 from crates.io. `cargo binstall` is not part of a Rust install. `cargo binstall eb_stack` fails with `no such command: binstall` until that program is installed on its own; it then installs the release binary. From this checkout: ```sh git clone https://github.com/stackhands/eb-stack.git cd eb-stack cargo build --locked --release install -Dm755 target/release/eb-stack ~/.local/bin/eb-stack ``` Add `~/.local/bin` to `PATH`. `eb-stack --version` then prints `eb-stack 0.7.4`. The test suite is `cargo test --locked`, in [Tests](#tests). It is not required before the first solve. Build the Rust binary on a suitable build host. EasyBuild installs belong on the target selected by the public target configuration, not necessarily on the machine running the CLI. Documentation: [https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me) ## Inspect from a fresh clone The repository includes foreign-recipe and package-config fixtures, so the parsing boundary can be exercised without an EasyBuild installation or external robot tree: ```sh eb-stack package inspect \ --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/conda_eon/recipe.yaml \ --format conda-forge \ --toolchain foss/2026.1 \ --package-config examples/packages/common.toml \ --package-config examples/packages/eon.toml \ --out-dir /tmp/eon-inspect python3 -m json.tool /tmp/eon-inspect/package.plan.json >/dev/null python3 -m json.tool /tmp/eon-inspect/package.sbom.cdx.json >/dev/null ``` This writes the canonical build manifest and planned CycloneDX SBOM. It does not solve dependencies, emit recipes, or make a build claim; those stages need an EasyBuild robot tree and a configured build target. ## Documentation The manual is organized around operator tasks: - [get started](docs/orgmode/get-started.org) on the bundled fixtures; - [installation](docs/orgmode/install.org) for Linux, macOS, Windows, crates.io, and a checkout; - [sharding and inode admission](docs/orgmode/explanation/sharding-admission.org); - [foreign recipe to verified package](docs/orgmode/tutorial.org); - [package bundle schemas](docs/orgmode/reference/package-bundles.org); - [layered build targets](docs/orgmode/reference/targets.org); - [campaign state and typed findings](docs/orgmode/reference/campaigns.org); - [repair a failed campaign](docs/orgmode/howto/repair-campaign.org); - [command-line reference](docs/orgmode/reference/cli.org); - [which modules carry a component](docs/orgmode/howto/component-reach.org), by name and version, by package URL, or by a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) id resolved through Open Source Vulnerabilities (OSV); - [what a dependency closure answers](docs/orgmode/explanation/sbom-blast-radius.org). The source manual lives in `docs/orgmode/`; the documentation workflow exports RST into `docs/source/` and validates the Sphinx site. ## Bump an existing recipe ```sh eb-stack package bump \ --source tests/repro_fixtures/gromacs/GROMACS-2024.4-foss-2023b.eb \ --toolchain foss/2024a \ --easyconfigs tests/repro_fixtures/universe_foss_2024a \ --out-dir /tmp/gromacs-2024a ``` The output recipe is `/tmp/gromacs-2024a/easyconfigs/g/GROMACS/GROMACS-2024.4-foss-2024a.eb`; the same directory contains its manifest, SBOM, and `default` profile lock. Repeat `--easyconfigs` for overlays and use `--stack-policy` for European Environment for Scientific Software Installations (EESSI) or site preferences. `preferred` pins may fall back inside Resolvo; `locked` pins may not. Known maintainer fixtures cover GROMACS, ScaFaCoS, MDTraj, Fiona, PuLP, and numba across `foss-2023b` to `foss-2024a`. ## Plan a new package Package policy is public, layered TOML. Parsers preserve foreign names and syntax without package-name branches; Resolvo matches case/punctuation-equivalent robot names mechanically. Explicit ecosystem aliases, EasyBuild metadata, build policy, and independently installable profiles live in package config. Each profile emits one `.eb` file; Message Passing Interface (MPI) and OpenMP toolchain options alone do not require a suffix. Profiles can declare `platform` and `architecture` target context. Foreign selectors are evaluated against those values before dependency solving, so a target-specific dependency becomes a real Resolvo requirement instead of disappearing with no message when planning runs on another host. The Spack adapter parses Python into an abstract syntax tree (AST) without importing the recipe. It statically evaluates literal data, bounded loops, formatting, and `when` scopes; unsupported runtime expressions become source-located residuals rather than guessed dependencies. Parser notes are informational. Planning consumes only typed residual records, so a note about successfully materializing dynamic source logic cannot accidentally enqueue Hermes work. Genuine residuals carry a category, severity, summary, and optional evidence and source provenance. Conda revision numbers and compiler/stdlib/cross-build template requirements are toolchain diagnostics rather than package-authoring work. Unknown templates inside ordinary package identities remain explicit residuals. Aliases use `foreign = "EasyBuild"` when both names share a version domain. Component-to-provider mappings use `foreign = { provider = "EasyBuild", constraint = "drop" }`, so a component release such as a Python package version is never imposed on its containing EasyBuild provider. Package policy also has two generic EasyBuild inputs: ```toml [build.easyconfig_parameters] general_packages = ["ASPHERE", "KSPACE", "MOLECULE"] [[build.patches]] filename = "Orbit-2.0-portability.patch" sha256 = "4f43b42fdcf84d0cf634d993dd944f252c8243dc612a919fe2825d56f937c8eb" source = "patches/Orbit-2.0-portability.patch" [[dependencies.requirements]] name = "VTK" roles = ["run"] ``` By default, a layer that declares `build.patches` replaces the preceding patch list. Set `patches_mode = "merge"` in `[build]` to preserve patches extracted from conda-forge or Spack while adding EasyBuild policy patches. A merged entry with the same filename replaces that artifact, so a reviewed checksum and source path can refine foreign metadata without creating a duplicate. Easyconfig parameters are typed data, not Python fragments. Requirements enter the canonical manifest and CycloneDX SBOM before Resolvo selects a version. Package planning requires every source and patch SHA-256; emitted checksums remain positional with sources first and patches second. Local patch assets are verified and copied beside every emitted recipe. Checksum-addressed remote patches retain their exact URL in `patches`; EasyBuild downloads and verifies them during the build. `scripts/fetch-upstream-trees.sh` creates a checkout of the pinned easybuilders trees. Source the `env.sh` it writes so `$EB_EASYCONFIGS` is the develop `easybuild/easyconfigs` directory. ```sh eb-stack package plan \ --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/conda_eon/recipe.yaml \ --format conda-forge \ --toolchain foss/2026.1 \ --package-config examples/packages/common.toml \ --package-config examples/packages/eon.toml \ --package-catalog examples/package-catalog/eon.toml \ --package-sources examples/package-sources/eon-companions.toml \ --easyconfigs "$EB_EASYCONFIGS" \ --easyconfigs fixtures/eon_foss_2026_1/easyconfigs \ --stack-policy examples/stacks/eon-foss-2026.1.toml \ --out-dir /tmp/eon ``` Against easybuild-easyconfigs develop `981d2123dd` that prints: ```text closure_plan=/tmp/eon/closure.plan.json closure_sbom=/tmp/eon/closure.sbom.cdx.json build_order=/tmp/eon/build-order.json manifest=/tmp/eon/package.plan.json sbom=/tmp/eon/package.sbom.cdx.json lock=/tmp/eon/locks/default.lock.json easyconfig=/tmp/eon/easyconfigs/e/eOn/eOn-2.16.0-foss-2026.1.eb patch=/tmp/eon/easyconfigs/e/eOn/eOn-2.16.0_safemath-eigen5-core-guard.patch companion_manifest=/tmp/eon/packages/readcon-core-0.13.1-GCCcore-15.2.0/package.plan.json companion_sbom=/tmp/eon/packages/readcon-core-0.13.1-GCCcore-15.2.0/package.sbom.cdx.json companion_lock=/tmp/eon/packages/readcon-core-0.13.1-GCCcore-15.2.0/locks/default.lock.json easyconfig=/tmp/eon/easyconfigs/r/readcon-core/readcon-core-0.13.1-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb companion_manifest=/tmp/eon/packages/rgpot-2.5.3-GCCcore-15.2.0/package.plan.json companion_sbom=/tmp/eon/packages/rgpot-2.5.3-GCCcore-15.2.0/package.sbom.cdx.json companion_lock=/tmp/eon/packages/rgpot-2.5.3-GCCcore-15.2.0/locks/default.lock.json easyconfig=/tmp/eon/easyconfigs/r/rgpot/rgpot-2.5.3-GCCcore-15.2.0.eb ``` Because `--easyconfigs` is also a discovery root, that plan writes `closure.plan.json`, `closure.sbom.cdx.json`, and `build-order.json` next to the manifest, even when no companion recipe was required. The included eOn package policy is **core + `with_rgpot`**: Fortran/CuH2 client, readcon-core, and in-process RGPOT (engines dlopen at runtime). Fat metatomic/xTB/serve are off by default; conda host deps for those names are excluded from the solve. The stack policy only prefers Eigen 5 for the safemath patch path. Historical full-product fixtures under `fixtures/eon_packaging` and `fixtures/eon_foss_2026_1` remain as regression snapshots of the old feedstock-parity surface. Use `--format spack`, `examples/packages/common.toml`, and `examples/packages/qmcpack.toml` for QMCPACK's `package.py`. Its Spack version is pinned by commit rather than archive hash, so planning also needs `--source-checksum 511d5f368db002f2f77504619e1ada8d4a3034200d25feef6773d12a6ed6d18e`. Parser output retains source spans, conda selectors, Spack conditions/conflicts, dependency roles, and residual dynamic logic. Inspect without solving or emitting recipes: ```sh eb-stack package inspect \ --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/spack_qmcpack/package.py \ --format spack \ --toolchain foss/2026.1 \ --package-config examples/packages/common.toml \ --package-config examples/packages/qmcpack.toml \ --out-dir /tmp/qmcpack-inspect ``` ## Check recipes ```sh eb-stack recipe format /tmp/eon/easyconfigs/e/eOn/*.eb eb-stack recipe lint /tmp/eon/easyconfigs/e/eOn/*.eb eb-stack recipe check \ --recipe /tmp/eon/easyconfigs/e/eOn/eOn-2.16.0-foss-2026.1.eb \ --easyconfigs /path/to/robot \ --easyconfigs /tmp/eon/easyconfigs ``` Checksums are positional: sources first, then patches. Missing dependency output includes compatible hierarchy members and candidates found in other generations. Fix the recipe or companion; do not bypass the check. ## Configure and run builds Targets are layered as transport to executor to runtime to EasyBuild workload: ```sh eb-stack target list --config examples/targets/base.toml --config ~/.config/eb-stack/site.toml eb-stack target doctor \ --config examples/targets/base.toml \ --config ~/.config/eb-stack/site.toml \ --target site-builder eb-stack campaign run \ --bundle /tmp/eon \ --config examples/targets/base.toml \ --config ~/.config/eb-stack/site.toml \ --target site-builder \ --state /tmp/eon.campaign.json ``` `campaign run` is a foreground command. Keep it under the site's normal terminal or service supervisor and inspect the state from another shell with `campaign status`. Only one run, claim, or resolution can write a state file at a time. The process lock releases automatically if the controlling process exits; before rerunning an interrupted state, confirm that its routed container, scheduler job, or host command is no longer active. Transport may be local or SSH; execution may be direct or Slurm; runtime may be host, Podman, or Docker. Site hostnames, paths, modules, and scheduler sizing belong in the site layer. Container targets must use ABI-specific install, work, and temporary roots; only source archives should be shared across runtimes. Cargo searches ancestor directories for `.cargo/config.toml`. If target storage lives below a bind-mounted home directory, mount the campaign subtree again at a neutral container path such as `/eb-stack-campaigns`, then use that path for runtime `workdir` and EasyBuild `work_root`. The [target reference](docs/orgmode/reference/targets.org) includes the complete TOML pattern. The runnable local target defaults to two parallel EasyBuild jobs so memory-heavy C++ compilations remain usable on common workstations. Treat `EASYBUILD_PARALLEL`, scheduler CPUs, and scheduler memory as one allocation: raise parallelism only when the target has measured headroom. A compiler process killed by the kernel or exhausted virtual memory is a retryable `resource` finding, not evidence that the selected dependency is incompatible. For a local public example, build `skills/new-package/container/rocky9/Containerfile`, populate `/tmp/eb-stack/robot`, and use `examples/targets/local-podman.toml`. Keep bundles below `/tmp/eb-stack/bundles` so host and container paths match. Hermes and OMP name campaign roles, not required orchestration software. Hermes is the single owner that reads typed findings, applies repairs, and retries through the requested claim rung. OMP workers are optional concurrent participants that coordinate exclusively through finding ownership. Campaign failures persist as typed findings. OMP workers coordinate repairs through owned queue operations: ```sh eb-stack campaign finding claim --state /tmp/eon.campaign.json \ --id attempt:1:finding:1 --owner omp-worker-1 eb-stack campaign finding resolve --state /tmp/eon.campaign.json \ --id attempt:1:finding:1 --owner omp-worker-1 \ --action "corrected package configuration" \ --evidence "recipe check exits successfully" \ --change examples/packages/eon.toml ``` The state file retains attempts, the active recipe, typed failure commands and compact logs, ownership, repair evidence, and the claim ladder. A successful retry supersedes the matching open finding. ## Solve a whole stack ```sh eb-stack stack solve \ --easyconfigs fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs \ --stack-policy fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/policies/prefer_newer.json \ --baseline-easyconfigs fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs \ --lock-out stack.lock.json \ --sbom-out stack.cdx.json \ --build-list-out build.list \ --stack-diff-out stack.diff.md ``` ## See which easyconfigs an easyblock change reaches ```sh eb-stack easyblock-reach \ --easyblocks ~/src/easybuild-easyblocks \ --easyconfigs ~/src/easybuild-easyconfigs \ --file ~/src/easybuild-easyblocks/easybuild/easyblocks/generic/cmakemake.py \ --reverse \ --out-dir /tmp/cmakemake-reach ``` A change to `CMakeMake` reaches recipes that name it, recipes whose `EB_` class subclasses it (GROMACS does), and extensions or bundle components that resolve to it. `--range A..B` and `--pr N` read the changed Python from a local clone (`refs/pull/N/head` for a pull request). `--reverse` adds modules that depend on a reached module. The report is `reach.toml`, `reach.json`, and `reach.md`. ## MCP - MCP Registry name: `mcp-name: io.github.stackhands/eb-stack` `eb-stack mcp` exposes the version-one workflows as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools over stdio, and one tool for `pr-overlap`, `rebuild-set`, `component-reach`, and `easyblock-reach`. `eb-stack mcp --workspace ROOT` (or `EB_STACK_WORKSPACE`) is the root for the recipe file tools. - `eb_package_inspect`, `eb_package_plan`, `eb_package_bump`, `eb_package_latest`; - `eb_recipe_read`, `eb_recipe_list`, `eb_recipe_edit`, `eb_recipe_write`, `eb_recipe_grep`, `eb_recipe_apply_suggestion`, `eb_recipe_diff`, `eb_dep_versions`; - `eb_recipe_easyblock`, `eb_recipe_templates`, `eb_recipe_hierarchy`; - `eb_recipe_check`, `eb_recipe_lint`, `eb_recipe_format`; - `eb_module_lint`, `eb_easyblock_dry_run`, `eb_build_log`, `eb_build_test` (easyblocks; `eb_build_test` only with `EB_STACK_ALLOW_BUILD=1`); - `eb_stack_solve`, `eb_stack_sbom`, `eb_stack_order`, `eb_stack_easystack`, `eb_stack_gap`, `eb_stack_provided`, `eb_stack_shadow`, `eb_stack_batch`, `eb_stack_shard`, `eb_stack_arch`, `eb_stack_files`, `eb_stack_generation`, `eb_stack_cuda_cc`, `eb_stack_known_failures`, `eb_stack_oom`, `eb_stack_bot_classify`, `eb_stack_sections`, `eb_stack_from_commit`; - `eb_component_reach` (same query as `component-reach`, including a purl or a CVE id); - `eb_target_list`, `eb_target_doctor`; - `eb_campaign_run`, `eb_campaign_status`; - `eb_campaign_finding_claim`, `eb_campaign_finding_resolve`; - `eb_pr_overlap` (`kind` `software-layer` or `easyconfigs`), `eb_rebuild_set`, `eb_easyblock_reach`; - `eb_repro_summary`. `eb_recipe_edit` replaces an exact string and does not write a repeated match unless `replace_all` is set. `eb_recipe_check` requires at least one `easyconfigs` path (a `.eb` there means its easyconfigs directory) and refuses a recipe that is not valid Python. `eb_recipe_lint` reports the easyconfigs CI lint (F541, W605, W291), the check-contrib pycodestyle codes, the easyconfigs test-suite checks and the review conventions (`EB_*`), plus E999 for syntax errors, with a `clean` flag; it does not rely on `eb --check-contrib` but merges it when `eb` is installed. `EB_STACK_EB` names the `eb` to run, and `EB_STACK_EB=none` skips that check with the report saying why, which keeps a lint deterministic on a host whose `eb` would judge a recipe the local checks accept. `eb_recipe_grep` searches the workspace. ## Skills Two produce recipes, three gate them, three carry them somewhere, one repairs the generator. Produce: - [New package](skills/new-package/SKILL.md): conda-forge/Spack to profiles to bundle to Hermes/OMP campaign. - [Annual bump](skills/annual-bump/SKILL.md): EasyBuild recipe to SBOM + Resolvo bump bundle to campaign. Gate, before anything is built or pushed: - [Verify recipe](skills/verify-recipe/SKILL.md): prove the checksum, the patches, the extension versions, the configure options and the dependency bounds against the real source, without spending a build. - [EasyBuild dos and don'ts](skills/easybuild-dos-donts/SKILL.md): recipe-shape rules and the pre-PR checklist behind `recipe check`. - [Easyblock fix](skills/easyblock-fix/SKILL.md): change an easyblock from an issue report, then prove it with the generated commands (`eb -x`) and a build that runs the test step. Carry: - [Upstream PR](skills/upstream-pr/SKILL.md): recipe set to maintainer-acceptable easybuild-easyconfigs PR, distilled from real merged and rejected PRs. - [Site consume](skills/site-consume/SKILL.md): build an upstream recipe at a site through `--from-pr` / `--from-commit` instead of forking it into the site's repository. - [EESSI extend](skills/eessi-extend/SKILL.md): test inside the EESSI compatibility layer and contribute to the software-layer easystacks. The public issue and PR surface belongs to the human operator. The skills produce recipe sets and evidence; they do not open or mutate upstream issues or PRs. ## Tests ```sh cargo test --locked --all-targets ``` The suite covers foreign syntax adapters, conditions, CycloneDX generation, profile materialization, stack-policy fallback, hierarchy-aware Resolvo locks, variant emission, known bump reproduction, target routing, persisted campaigns, binary verification, finding ownership, CLI, and MCP. ## License [MIT](LICENSE) · [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md) · [Security](SECURITY.md) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) ## Ledger event retries A producer can retain one JSON event packet with a unique `build.event_id` and retry `ledger append` with that same packet. An identical retry acknowledges the recorded entry and signs the current head without adding another line. Different content under the same identifier is refused. The identifier belongs to one event, including its operation stage. A failed signed-head write can occur after the record is durable. Retaining the packet makes that failure recoverable without duplicating the event. An acknowledged retry accepts `--expect-head` only when it matches a prefix of the current history. A new append still requires the exact current head. Head signature trust is checked through `ledger verify`; the expected-head argument is an optimistic history check. ## Part of stackhands eb-stack is one of the [stackhands](https://github.com/stackhands) tools for building, installing and maintaining an HPC software stack with EasyBuild on top of EESSI. | Tool | Job | Docs | |---|---|---| | **eb-stack** | Solve, shard and plan an EasyBuild build list; admit builds under a scratch inode budget | [docs](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/) | | [eb-staged-rebuild](https://github.com/stackhands/eb-staged-rebuild) | Rebuild an installation in a staged tree and swap it in, so running jobs keep their paths | [docs](https://stackhands.github.io/eb-staged-rebuild/) | | [eessi-arch-guard](https://github.com/stackhands/eessi-arch-guard) | Reload EESSI in a Slurm task that inherited it for another CPU or GPU | [docs](https://stackhands.github.io/eessi-arch-guard/) | | [eb-local](https://github.com/stackhands/eb-local) | Install software with EasyBuild on top of EESSI into a directory a user or project owns | [docs](https://stackhands.github.io/eb-local/) | | [eb-keep-logs](https://github.com/stackhands/eb-keep-logs) | Keep a failed build's EasyBuild log and command output; rotate a pipeline's log tree | [docs](https://stackhands.github.io/eb-keep-logs/) | | [rfc9162](https://github.com/stackhands/rfc9162) | Append-only Merkle logs hashed as RFC 9162, with tiled storage and signed checkpoints | [docs](https://stackhands.github.io/rfc9162/) | | [zig-common](https://github.com/stackhands/zig-common) | The shared Zig library under the Zig tools: system calls, checked files, child processes | [docs](https://stackhands.github.io/zig-common/) |

**Turn foreign and EasyBuild recipes into resolved, build-evaluated package bundles.** `eb-stack` parses conda-forge, Spack, PyPI, Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN), Cargo, LuaRocks, Raku, and EasyBuild recipes into one canonical package plan. It emits a planned CycloneDX Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), solves each product profile with Resolvo, writes one conventional `.eb` file per installable variant, and drives the recipes through a persisted remote build campaign. A plan is not a build. `package plan` and `package bump` can establish only **resolves**. `campaign run` owns **builds** and **binary-verified**. The GitHub release and the crates.io package are 0.7.4 and carry every command here. The [glossary](docs/orgmode/reference/glossary.org) defines closure, generation, baseline, and reachability. The longer path is the [tutorial](docs/orgmode/tutorial.org). [![CI](https://github.com/stackhands/eb-stack/actions/workflows/ci_test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/stackhands/eb-stack/actions/workflows/ci_test.yml) [![Docs](https://github.com/stackhands/eb-stack/actions/workflows/ci_docs.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/stackhands/eb-stack/actions/workflows/ci_docs.yml) [![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/eb_stack.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/eb_stack) [![docs](https://img.shields.io/badge/docs-eb--stack.rgoswami.me-blue)](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE) ## Discovery - [llms.txt](llms.txt) indexes the manual. [llms-full.txt](llms-full.txt) repeats every page in one file. - [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) describes contribution and validation requirements. - The skills for inspect, plan, bump, a stack SBOM, pull-request overlap, and the stdio server are under [skills/](skills/). - The Model Context Protocol manifest is [server.json](server.json). Client configuration is the manual page [Model Context Protocol server](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/reference/mcp.html). ## Pipeline

```text conda-forge / Spack / EasyBuild │ ▼ canonical package.plan.json ─── package.sbom.cdx.json │ ▼ profile materialization + stack policy + Resolvo │ ├── locks/.lock.json └── easyconfigs///.eb │ ▼ target-routed campaign + typed findings ``` New packages and bumps use the same artifacts. A bump is an EasyBuild-origin plan plus SBOM and Resolvo lock, not a standalone text rewrite. ## Claim ladder

Report these claims independently: 1. **resolves**: every requested profile has a Resolvo lock and emitted recipe; 2. **builds**: every emitted recipe completes through EasyBuild on the configured target; 3. **binary-verified**: every declared profile verification command succeeds. `package inspect` establishes none of them. `package plan` and `package bump` can establish only `resolves`. `campaign run` owns the other two. ## Install The crate is `eb_stack` on crates.io; the installed binary is `eb-stack`. Rust 1.90 or newer is required when building from source. `rustc` 1.83 stops while reading the crate index: the Cargo feature `edition2024` is not stabilized. `rustup toolchain install stable` and `rustup default stable` provide a new enough compiler. The GitHub release is 0.7.4, with installers and archives for Linux (x86-64, aarch64), macOS and Windows, and `eb-stack --version` prints `0.7.4` for it, as a build of this tree does. `cargo install eb_stack --locked` builds the same 0.7.4 from crates.io. `cargo binstall` is not part of a Rust install. `cargo binstall eb_stack` fails with `no such command: binstall` until that program is installed on its own; it then installs the release binary. From this checkout: ```sh git clone https://github.com/stackhands/eb-stack.git cd eb-stack cargo build --locked --release install -Dm755 target/release/eb-stack ~/.local/bin/eb-stack ``` Add `~/.local/bin` to `PATH`. `eb-stack --version` then prints `eb-stack 0.7.4`. The test suite is `cargo test --locked`, in [Tests](#tests). It is not required before the first solve. Build the Rust binary on a suitable build host. EasyBuild installs belong on the target selected by the public target configuration, not necessarily on the machine running the CLI. Documentation: [https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me) ## Inspect from a fresh clone The repository includes foreign-recipe and package-config fixtures, so the parsing boundary can be exercised without an EasyBuild installation or external robot tree: ```sh eb-stack package inspect \ --source fixtures/foreign_ingest/conda_eon/recipe.yaml \ --format conda-forge \ --toolchain foss/2026.1 \ --package-config examples/packages/common.toml \ --package-config examples/packages/eon.toml \ --out-dir /tmp/eon-inspect python3 -m json.tool /tmp/eon-inspect/package.plan.json >/dev/null python3 -m json.tool /tmp/eon-inspect/package.sbom.cdx.json >/dev/null ``` This writes the canonical build manifest and planned CycloneDX SBOM. It does not solve dependencies, emit recipes, or make a build claim; those stages need an EasyBuild robot tree and a configured build target. ## Documentation The manual is organized around operator tasks: - [get started](docs/orgmode/get-started.org) on the bundled fixtures; - [installation](docs/orgmode/install.org) for Linux, macOS, Windows, crates.io, and a checkout; - [sharding and inode admission](docs/orgmode/explanation/sharding-admission.org); - [foreign recipe to verified package](docs/orgmode/tutorial.org); - [package bundle schemas](docs/orgmode/reference/package-bundles.org); - [layered build targets](docs/orgmode/reference/targets.org); - [campaign state and typed findings](docs/orgmode/reference/campaigns.org); - [repair a failed campaign](docs/orgmode/howto/repair-campaign.org); - [command-line reference](docs/orgmode/reference/cli.org); - [which modules carry a component](docs/orgmode/howto/component-reach.org), by name and version, by package URL, or by a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) id resolved through Open Source Vulnerabilities (OSV); - [what a dependency closure answers](docs/orgmode/explanation/sbom-blast-radius.org). Repeat `--easyconfigs` for overlays and use `--stack-policy` for European Environment for Scientific Software Installations (EESSI) or site preferences. `preferred` pins may fall back inside Resolvo; `locked` pins may not. Known maintainer fixtures cover GROMACS, ScaFaCoS, MDTraj, Fiona, PuLP, and numba across `foss-2023b` to `foss-2024a`. ## Plan a new package Package policy is public, layered TOML. Parsers preserve foreign names and syntax without package-name branches; Resolvo matches case/punctuation-equivalent robot names mechanically. Explicit ecosystem aliases, EasyBuild metadata, build policy, and independently installable profiles live in package config. Each profile emits one `.eb` file; Message Passing Interface (MPI) and OpenMP toolchain options alone do not require a suffix. Profiles can declare `platform` and `architecture` target context. Foreign selectors are evaluated against those values before dependency solving, so a target-specific dependency becomes a real Resolvo requirement instead of disappearing with no message when planning runs on another host. The Spack adapter parses Python into an abstract syntax tree (AST) without importing the recipe. It statically evaluates literal data, bounded loops, formatting, and `when` scopes; unsupported runtime expressions become source-located residuals rather than guessed dependencies. Parser notes are informational. Planning consumes only typed residual records, so a note about successfully materializing dynamic source logic cannot accidentally enqueue Hermes work. Genuine residuals carry a category, severity, summary, and optional evidence and source provenance. Conda revision numbers and compiler/stdlib/cross-build template requirements are toolchain diagnostics rather than package-authoring work. Unknown templates inside ordinary package identities remain explicit residuals. Aliases use `foreign = "EasyBuild"` when both names share a version domain. Local patch assets are verified and copied beside every emitted recipe. OMP workers are optional concurrent participants that coordinate exclusively through finding ownership. Campaign failures persist as typed findings. OMP workers coordinate repairs through owned queue operations: ```sh eb-stack campaign finding claim --state /tmp/eon.campaign.json \ --id attempt:1:finding:1 --owner omp-worker-1 eb-stack campaign finding resolve --state /tmp/eon.campaign.json \ --id attempt:1:finding:1 --owner omp-worker-1 \ --action "corrected package configuration" \ --evidence "recipe check exits successfully" \ --change examples/packages/eon.toml ``` The state file retains attempts, the active recipe, typed failure commands and compact logs, ownership, repair evidence, and the claim ladder. A successful retry supersedes the matching open finding. ## Solve a whole stack ```sh eb-stack stack solve \ --easyconfigs fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs \ --stack-policy fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/policies/prefer_newer.json \ --baseline-easyconfigs fixtures/gromacs_2025_to_next/easyconfigs \ --lock-out stack.lock.json \ --sbom-out stack.cdx.json \ --build-list-out build.list \ --stack-diff-out stack.diff.md ``` ## See which easyconfigs an easyblock change reaches ```sh eb-stack easyblock-reach \ --easyblocks ~/src/easybuild-easyblocks \ --easyconfigs ~/src/easybuild-easyconfigs \ --file ~/src/easybuild-easyblocks/easybuild/easyblocks/generic/cmakemake.py \ --reverse \ --out-dir /tmp/cmakemake-reach ``` A change to `CMakeMake` reaches recipes that name it, recipes whose `EB_` class subclasses it (GROMACS does), and extensions or bundle components that resolve to it. `--range A..B` and `--pr N` read the changed Python from a local clone (`refs/pull/N/head` for a pull request). `--reverse` adds modules that depend on a reached module. The report is `reach.toml`, `reach.json`, and `reach.md`. ## MCP - MCP Registry name: `mcp-name: io.github.stackhands/eb-stack` `eb-stack mcp` exposes the version-one workflows as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools over stdio, and one tool for `pr-overlap`, `rebuild-set`, `component-reach`, and `easyblock-reach`. `eb-stack mcp --workspace ROOT` (or `EB_STACK_WORKSPACE`) is the root for the recipe file tools. - `eb_package_inspect`, `eb_package_plan`, `eb_package_bump`, `eb_package_latest`; - `eb_recipe_read`, `eb_recipe_list`, `eb_recipe_edit`, `eb_recipe_write`, `eb_recipe_grep`, `eb_recipe_apply_suggestion`, `eb_recipe_diff`, `eb_dep_versions`; - `eb_recipe_easyblock`, `eb_recipe_templates`, `eb_recipe_hierarchy`; - `eb_recipe_check`, `eb_recipe_lint`, `eb_recipe_format`; - `eb_module_lint`, `eb_easyblock_dry_run`, `eb_build_log`, `eb_build_test` (easyblocks; `eb_build_test` only with `EB_STACK_ALLOW_BUILD=1`); - `eb_stack_solve`, `eb_stack_sbom`, `eb_stack_order`, `eb_stack_easystack`, `eb_stack_gap`, `eb_stack_provided`, `eb_stack_shadow`, `eb_stack_batch`, `eb_stack_shard`, `eb_stack_arch`, `eb_stack_files`, `eb_stack_generation`, `eb_stack_cuda_cc`, `eb_stack_known_failures`, `eb_stack_oom`, `eb_stack_bot_classify`, `eb_stack_sections`, `eb_stack_from_commit`; - `eb_component_reach` (same query as `component-reach`, including a purl or a CVE id); - `eb_target_list`, `eb_target_doctor`; - `eb_campaign_run`, `eb_campaign_status`; - `eb_campaign_finding_claim`, `eb_campaign_finding_resolve`; - `eb_pr_overlap` (`kind` `software-layer` or `easyconfigs`), `eb_rebuild_set`, `eb_easyblock_reach`; - `eb_repro_summary`. `eb_recipe_edit` replaces an exact string and does not write a repeated match unless `replace_all` is set. `eb_recipe_check` requires at least one `easyconfigs` path (a `.eb` there means its easyconfigs directory) and refuses a recipe that is not valid Python. `eb_recipe_lint` reports the easyconfigs CI lint (F541, W605, W291), the check-contrib pycodestyle codes, the easyconfigs test-suite checks and the review conventions (`EB_*`), plus E999 for syntax errors, with a `clean` flag; it does not rely on `eb --check-contrib` but merges it when `eb` is installed. `EB_STACK_EB` names the `eb` to run, and `EB_STACK_EB=none` skips that check with the report saying why, which keeps a lint deterministic on a host whose `eb` would judge a recipe the local checks accept. `eb_recipe_grep` searches the workspace. ## Skills Two produce recipes, three gate them, three carry them somewhere, one repairs the generator. Produce: - [New package](skills/new-package/SKILL.md): conda-forge/Spack to profiles to bundle to Hermes/OMP campaign. - [Annual bump](skills/annual-bump/SKILL.md): EasyBuild recipe to SBOM + Resolvo bump bundle to campaign. Gate, before anything is built or pushed: - [Verify recipe](skills/verify-recipe/SKILL.md): prove the checksum, the patches, the extension versions, the configure options and the dependency bounds against the real source, without spending a build. - [EasyBuild dos and don'ts](skills/easybuild-dos-donts/SKILL.md): recipe-shape rules and the pre-PR checklist behind `recipe check`. - [Easyblock fix](skills/easyblock-fix/SKILL.md): change an easyblock from an issue report, then prove it with the generated commands (`eb -x`) and a build that runs the test step. Carry: - [Upstream PR](skills/upstream-pr/SKILL.md): recipe set to maintainer-acceptable easybuild-easyconfigs PR, distilled from real merged and rejected PRs. - [Site consume](skills/site-consume/SKILL.md): build an upstream recipe at a site through `--from-pr` / `--from-commit` instead of forking it into the site's repository. - [EESSI extend](skills/eessi-extend/SKILL.md): test inside the EESSI compatibility layer and contribute to the software-layer easystacks. Repair: - [Tool repair](skills/tool-repair/SKILL.md): a hand correction to emitted output is a bug report; fix eb-stack, regression-test it on the remote builder, regenerate, and diff byte-for-byte. The public issue and PR surface belongs to the human operator. The skills produce recipe sets and evidence; they do not open or mutate upstream issues or PRs. ## Tests ```sh cargo test --locked --all-targets ``` The suite covers foreign syntax adapters, conditions, CycloneDX generation, profile materialization, stack-policy fallback, hierarchy-aware Resolvo locks, variant emission, known bump reproduction, target routing, persisted campaigns, binary verification, finding ownership, CLI, and MCP. ## License [MIT](LICENSE) · [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md) · [Security](SECURITY.md) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) ## Ledger event retries A producer can retain one JSON event packet with a unique `build.event_id` and retry `ledger append` with that same packet. An identical retry acknowledges the recorded entry and signs the current head without adding another line. Different content under the same identifier is refused. The identifier belongs to one event, including its operation stage. A failed signed-head write can occur after the record is durable. Retaining the packet makes that failure recoverable without duplicating the event. An acknowledged retry accepts `--expect-head` only when it matches a prefix of the current history. A new append still requires the exact current head. Head signature trust is checked through `ledger verify`; the expected-head argument is an optimistic history check. ## Part of stackhands eb-stack is one of the [stackhands](https://github.com/stackhands) tools for building, installing and maintaining an HPC software stack with EasyBuild on top of EESSI. | Tool | Job | Docs | |---|---|---| | **eb-stack** | Solve, shard and plan an EasyBuild build list; admit builds under a scratch inode budget | [docs](https://eb-stack.rgoswami.me/) | | [eb-staged-rebuild](https://github.com/stackhands/eb-staged-rebuild) | Rebuild an installation in a staged tree and swap it in, so running jobs keep their paths | [docs](https://stackhands.github.io/eb-staged-rebuild/) | | [eessi-arch-guard](https://github.com/stackhands/eessi-arch-guard) | Reload EESSI in a Slurm task that inherited it for another CPU or GPU | [docs](https://stackhands.github.io/eessi-arch-guard/) | | [eb-local](https://github.com/stackhands/eb-local) | Install software with EasyBuild on top of EESSI into a directory a user or project owns | [docs](https://stackhands.github.io/eb-local/) | | [eb-keep-logs](https://github.com/stackhands/eb-keep-logs) | Keep a failed build's EasyBuild log and command output; rotate a pipeline's log tree | [docs](https://stackhands.github.io/eb-keep-logs/) | | [rfc9162](https://github.com/stackhands/rfc9162) | Append-only Merkle logs hashed as RFC 9162, with tiled storage and signed checkpoints | [docs](https://stackhands.github.io/rfc9162/) | | [zig-common](https://github.com/stackhands/zig-common) | The shared Zig library under the Zig tools: system calls, checked files, child processes | [docs](https://stackhands.github.io/zig-common/) |

repository.description: Local-first .NET agent built on Starling models, with a calibrated decision fabric (Kev, GLiNER2, embeddings) and Corvid Vault for secrets the model never sees.
repository.name: corvid
repository.readme:
# Corvid **A local-first .NET 10 agent that thinks small on your machine and writes big wherever you choose.** Corvid is an agent in the spirit of Hermes Agent, built on [Starling](https://github.com/starlinghq/starling)'s in-process models. It splits the work in two: - **System One: the decision fabric.** Kev, GLiNER2 and the embedding models run in-process and make the many small calls an agent makes every turn: what the user wants, which tool fits, whether a step is risky, whether to escalate. These calls are local, fast and calibrated. - **System Two: the generator.** A swappable model, local (Qwen3.5-0.8B by default, or any OpenAI-compatible server) or cloud (Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Gemini), does the writing. Secrets never enter the agent. They live in **Corvid Vault**, a separate process that runs no model and swaps placeholders for real values only on the way out to the host each secret is bound to.


The windowed app, corvid-app --demo: a steer taken mid-turn, an approval card with every target and the reasons Kev asks, a patch to the launcher denied, then the palette, the Board and Rewind. The demo is a scripted scenario and needs no models (try it).

Website: [corvid.starling.rocks](https://corvid.starling.rocks) ## Contents - [Quick start](#quick-start) - [What Corvid does](#what-corvid-does) - [The windowed app](#the-windowed-app) - [Ways to talk to it](#ways-to-talk-to-it) - [Configuration](#configuration) - [Status](#status) - [Build and test](#build-and-test) - [Repository layout](#repository-layout) ## Quick start > **Release status.** The latest release, `v0.1.0` (2026-10-23), has the command line only. The windowed app and most of > what this README describes since (switching models mid-turn, subagents with a model mix, code mode, workspaces, > images, attached mode) are on `main` and come with the next release. Until then, `install.sh --app` stops because the > release has no `corvid-app-linux-x64.tar.gz`, and those features need a [source build](#from-source). Install the latest release (Linux x86_64; no .NET SDK needed): ```sh curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/starlinghq/corvid/main/install.sh | sh ``` It puts `corvid` and `corvid-vault` in `~/.local/bin`, with `corvid-sandbox` beside them in `~/.local/lib/corvid//`, after checking the download against the release's `SHA256SUMS`. Add `sh -s -- --cuda` for the CUDA variant (Kev on an NVIDIA GPU, about 300 MB more), `--version v0.1.0` for a given release, or `--prefix ` to install elsewhere. Running it again upgrades. Shell tools also need bubblewrap (`pacman -S bubblewrap`, `apt install bubblewrap`). Then: ```sh corvid doctor # what is missing, and how to fix it corvid model download qwen3.5-0.8b gliner2-base-v1 embeddinggemma-2 kev-0.8b # the default models (about 10 GB); nothing downloads implicitly corvid chat ``` Optional: `corvid model download kev-4b`, a second decision tier for gates (about 17 GB, 18 GB of RAM). Without Kev downloaded, decisions run on the degraded tier and `corvid chat` says so. The windowed app, `corvid-app`, installs with `--app`: ```sh curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/starlinghq/corvid/main/install.sh | sh -s -- --app ``` It goes beside `corvid` in `~/.local/lib/corvid//app/` with its own copy of `corvid-sandbox`, is linked as `~/.local/bin/corvid-app`, and gets a desktop entry (`~/.local/share/applications/corvid-app.desktop`) and the Corvid mark as its icon, so it shows as Corvid in the applications menu. It runs on the same Corvid home as `corvid chat`, and opens on First run while models are missing. `corvid doctor` says whether it is installed. ### Try the app without models `corvid-app --demo` runs the app on a scripted scenario with demo services and a frozen clock: no models, no Corvid home, nothing written. Send a message to start it moving, as in the recording above. From a source checkout: ```sh dotnet restore Corvid.slnx # once: the app builds corvid-sandbox, which only the solution restores dotnet run --project src/Corvid.App -c Release -- --demo # add --theme dark, --page board, or --scene approval ``` ### From source Requires the .NET 10 SDK ([build and test](#build-and-test)). Use `dotnet run --project src/Corvid.Cli -- ` in place of `corvid` and `dotnet run --project src/Corvid.App -c Release` in place of `corvid-app` (after `dotnet restore Corvid.slnx` once), or build the binaries yourself: ```sh dotnet publish src/Corvid.Cli -c Release -r linux-x64 # a single-file `corvid` dotnet publish src/Corvid.Cli -c Release -r linux-x64 -p:UseCuda=true -o out-cli-cuda # the CUDA variant, for Kev on an NVIDIA GPU ``` Releases are cut by pushing a `v*` tag; [`release.yml`](.github/workflows/release.yml) builds the CLI tarballs and the app's (`corvid-app-linux-x64.tar.gz`, from the `CorvidAppTarball` target in [`src/Corvid.App`](src/Corvid.App/README.md)), installs each with `install.sh` as a smoke test, and publishes them. ## What Corvid does ### Decides locally, writes wherever you choose Each turn starts with Kev answering a catalogue of small questions: intent, difficulty, whether to clarify, whether recall is needed, which tool. Kev's answers are calibrated against versioned floors. A confident answer acts. An unsure one asks or escalates. Gate questions can go to a second tier, Kev-4B. A hard step can go to a bigger generator slot, local or cloud. An embedding shortlist keeps the tool list the model sees short. Kev answers a checkpoint in about a quarter of a second on an RTX 3090 and in a few seconds on a CPU ([spike S1](docs/spikes/S1-kev-latency.md)). On CPU-only hosts Corvid asks fewer questions: at most two per step, and no per-call `risk` question where the outcome would be "ask" anyway. → [Decision fabric](docs/architecture.md#decision-fabric-c-004a) · [Kev decider](docs/architecture.md#kev-decider-c-004b) · [Kev on CUDA](docs/architecture.md#kev-on-cuda-c-029) ### Switches models at any time `/model` and the app's Models page switch a model mid-conversation, for any slot, the decider included; `Alt+P` in the app switches the generator. A running turn takes the switch at its next step, after the tool calls it has issued. The choice lasts for the session: escalation and fallback can still move off it, and the session comes back to it. `--default` changes the default for new sessions instead. Every switch is logged and shown in the transcript, and a cloud model is only ever reached through the privacy gate, with the session's taint. With `Corvid:Turn:ArchitectEditor` on, a coding turn that escalates is planned by the stronger model, with no tools, and its edits are made by the session's own model. `/architect` asks for that on the next turn, coding or not, and needs an escalation ladder. The transcript says "planned by X · edited by Y". → [Model slots and switching](docs/architecture.md#model-slots-and-switching-c-006) · [Architect/editor turns](docs/architecture.md#architecteditor-turns-a7) ### Delegates to subagents with their own model mix `delegate_task` starts child sessions, up to 10 at once and one level deep, each with a goal, an explicit toolset no wider than the parent's, a budget of steps, tokens and time, and an optional JSON schema its answer is checked against. The agent can give each child a model mix: any slot but the decider, from the catalogue, or a named mix from `Corvid:Agents:Mixes`. A child inherits its parent's taint and approval mode, its approvals come to you, and a cloud model in its mix passes the parent's privacy gate. The agent cannot choose the decider that judges a child's calls; only you or a configured mix can. A child cannot ask you questions, write memory, send messages, schedule jobs or delegate again. Children show as a tree on the Board, `/agents` lists them, and `/delegate` starts one yourself. ### Writes scripts that call its tools With code mode on (`Corvid:Tools:Code:Enabled`, and a cloud or local-server generator), `execute_code` runs a Python, JavaScript or C# script in the shell's sandbox, with no network. The script gets a generated client for Corvid's tools and reaches them only through a socket made for that run. Each call it makes goes through the same path as the model's own: its own approval, checkpoint, taint and credential scrub. The script itself always asks, with "once" as the only answer, and only the exact source you saw runs. Time, call count and output are limited on Corvid's side, and scripts can never reach a tool that delegates, asks, sends, schedules or writes memory. → [Code mode](docs/architecture.md#code-mode-foundation-a7) ### Asks before it acts, and explains why The app's approval card, with the Decisions panel listing each of Kev's answers and its confidence (corvid-app --scene approval). In corvid chat the same prompt is answered inline: once, this session, always, or deny. Every side effect goes through a structural approval pipeline. It parses the shell command (a bash subset, with wrappers such as `sudo`, `env` and `xargs` unwrapped), extracts every target, and checks the result against a hardline deny list before any model is asked. In **Smart** mode a call runs unasked only when Kev rates it low risk and it stays in the workspace, with no network, elevation or destructive tool. **Manual** mode asks for everything. - **Taint.** Once outside content (a web page, an MCP result, a guest's message) enters the session, even network reads go through approval, and any network egress or send to a new recipient always asks, offering only "once". - **Sandbox.** Shell commands run under `corvid-sandbox`: the workspace is writable, the rest of the system is read-only, credential stores are hidden, and there is no network unless allowed. Stdio MCP servers get a private workspace of their own. Allowed HTTPS goes through Vault's per-sandbox proxy, so a script can use a token it never sees. - **Detection rules.** A built-in pack of twelve rules watches the session event log before every approval. Examples: a credential read followed by network egress, the environment or a credential file sent out, base64 in a request URL, a command you just denied proposed again. A match on an enforce rule always asks, whatever the mode or remembered approvals say. → [Approvals](docs/architecture.md#approvals-c-007b) · [Sandbox](docs/architecture.md#sandbox-c-007a) · [Detection rules](docs/architecture.md#detection-rules-c-023) ### Undoes its own work, not yours The app's Rewind page (demo). In corvid chat the same restore is /undo and /rollback N. Before any tool call that changes files, Corvid checkpoints the workspace into a shadow git store, which is never your own repository. `/undo` reverts the last turn. `/rollback N` goes back to before the Nth latest checkpoint and takes those turns out of the conversation too. If you edited a file since, the revert becomes a three-way merge, and a conflict stops the restore so your edit is never overwritten. Checkpoints need `git` on `PATH`. `/fork` starts a new session from this one, even while a turn runs: it copies the log through the last completed step and the turn goes on untouched. Each session records its own workspace, so one window can hold several, and resuming a session from another directory still works where it began. `/workspace new` makes a git worktree on a `corvid/` branch, always asking first and never touching your checkout, and `delegate_task` can give a child a worktree of its own. → [Checkpoints](docs/architecture.md#checkpoints-c-014) ### Sees images, and can be steered mid-turn Paste or drop an image in the app, use `/image ` or `@shot.png` in `corvid chat`, or send one over ACP. Images go to a model that reads them, or are described by the vision slot; metadata is stripped first, and a cloud model gets one only if its egress policy allows it. `Ctrl+Enter` in the app steers a running turn: the message is taken at the next step, and goes to the queue if the turn ends first. The agent can ask you a clarifying question with `ask_user`, and in the app or `corvid chat` the turn waits for your answer. ### Remembers, and learns skills it has proven - **Memory.** Core blocks, episodic full-text search, a vector index and a bi-temporal fact graph, searched together. Writes are gated: a new fact is *staged* for you to approve in `/memory pending`, unless a calibrated decider allows it. - **Lessons.** Per-project lessons sit between facts and skills, with a quality bar and review. - **Skills.** Skills are [agentskills.io](https://agentskills.io) `SKILL.md` files in a git-versioned store, with authorship marked `user`, `agent` or `hub:`. Corvid drafts a new skill from a successful task, replays it as a test, and saves it only if the replay passes. `~/.hermes/skills` and Hermes' `MEMORY.md`/`USER.md` import for review. - **Consolidation.** When you are idle, a background job proposes shorter rewrites of core blocks near their budget. Nothing applies without your review, and a local-only block never reaches a cloud model. `/memory consolidate` asks now. - **Compaction.** Long sessions compact into a structured record with map-reduce summaries. The standing `/goal` is re-injected, and `/compact ` keeps what you name in full. - **Sessions.** Conversations get generated titles (`/rename` changes one), recaps on request or after an absence, and pins. `/search` searches what was said across them, leaving out gateway chats and job runs. → [Memory store](docs/architecture.md#memory-store-c-008) · [Sleep-time jobs](docs/architecture.md#sleep-time-memory-jobs-a7) · [Lessons](docs/architecture.md#lessons-and-project-scope-c-025) · [Skills](docs/architecture.md#skills-c-017) · [Compaction](docs/architecture.md#compaction-c-016) ### Keeps secrets out of the agent - **Vault-only keys.** Cloud model keys, MCP tokens and bot tokens are Vault secrets, each bound to its host. Corvid never reads keys from the environment, and without Vault cloud models are unavailable. - **Privacy egress gate.** Requests to cloud models are redacted by default (PII and any credential value). The egress ledger keeps each request as it was sent: `corvid egress`, or the app's Audit page, shows what left the machine. - **Credential scrub.** A token or password a tool returns, or one you paste into a message, is scrubbed before it reaches the event log, memory or any model (so the model sees a marker, not the secret: keep secrets in Vault). Memory and skills refuse one outright. - **Poisoned MCP tools.** MCP tool definitions are pinned on first listing. A tool that changes later, or whose description reads like injected instructions, is held until you review it. → [Vault](vault/README.md) · [Cloud slots and privacy egress](docs/architecture.md#cloud-slots-and-privacy-egress-c-015) · [Credential scrub](docs/architecture.md#credential-scrub-at-the-event-log-and-memory-c-040) · [MCP pinning](docs/architecture.md#mcp-tool-pinning-and-poisoned-descriptions-c-022) ### Runs jobs on a schedule `cron_create` and its siblings put durable jobs on a schedule. The scheduler wakes on a change or when a session opens, and each job's run reports back where it was created, including a chat on the gateway, and works in that session's workspace. `/cron` lists jobs, `/cron runs` shows their history, and you can pause, resume or remove one. → [Built-in tools and scheduler](docs/architecture.md#built-in-tools-and-scheduler-c-012) ### Leaves an audit trail Everything a session does is an append-only SQLite event log, and the session state is a projection of it. `corvid scan` runs the detection rules over the whole log afterwards. Add `--fail-on high` and it exits 4 on a serious finding, which suits CI. `corvid traces export` writes sessions in the JSONL telemetry schema of [Beacon](https://github.com/Asymptote-Labs/agent-beacon), so Beacon's detections and SIEM forwarding read Corvid like any other agent. OpenTelemetry spans cover the rest. → [Session event log](docs/architecture.md#session-event-log-c-002) · [Trace export](docs/architecture.md#trace-export-and-hermes-memory-import-c-027) ### Built-in tools and slash commands | Tools the model can call | | | --- | --- | | Files, confined to the workspace | `read_file`, `write_file`, `patch_file`, `list_files`, `search_files` | | Shell and web | `shell` (sandboxed, approved), `web_fetch` | | Code mode, when enabled | `execute_code` | | Subagents and questions | `delegate_task`, `ask_user` | | Memory | `memory_search`, `memory_add`, `memory_pending`, `memory_approve`, `memory_reject` | | Schedule | `cron_create`, `cron_list`, `cron_pause`, `cron_resume`, `cron_remove` | | Skills | `skill_list` and the skill tools | | From MCP servers | `server__tool`, asking before each call unless the server is trusted | | In chat | | | --- | --- | | `/help` `/status` `/tools` `/todos` | the commands, slots with device and latency, the tools with their risk, the session's todo list | | `/model` `/model ` | the generator's (or a slot's) models, numbered, with the current one and what each needs; type a number on the next line to switch | | `/model [slot] [--pin \| --default]` | switch a slot for this session, also while a turn runs; `--pin` holds it at a turn's end (escalation can still move it), `--default` sets the default for new sessions | | `/model unpin ` `/model reset ` | drop a pin; forget this session's choice | | `/architect [on \| off \| status]` | plan the next turn (or every turn) with the stronger model, then edit with this one | | `/goal [text \| clear]` | the standing goal, re-injected across compaction | | `/agents [show \| stop ]` `/delegate` | this session's child sessions; start one with `--mix`, `--model =`, `--tools`, `--toolset` and a budget | | `/sessions` `/search` `/rename` `/recap` `/pin` | recent conversations, search across them, this session's title, a recap, and keeping it at the top | | `/fork []` `/workspace` | fork this session, also during a turn; list, open, create or remove workspaces and worktrees | | `/approvals` | pending approvals and remembered approval rules | | `/memory` `/skills` | review staged memory, lessons and skill drafts; `/memory consolidate`; import from Hermes | | `/mcp` (`diff`, `accept`, `allow`) | servers, their tools, and held tool definitions | | `/undo` `/rollback [N]` | revert the last turn, or go back to a checkpoint | | `/compact [focus]` `/cron` | compact now; scheduled jobs and their runs | | `/image ` | attach an image to the next message (`corvid chat`) | | `/cancel` `/exit` | cancel the running turn; leave | In the composer, `# text` sends a fact through memory's gated write path, staged for review unless Kev allows it, `! command` runs a command yourself through the same sandbox and approvals, and `!! command` does so and keeps it out of what the model sees. `\#` and `\!` send the line as a message. ## The windowed app The Board (demo): every session and job run, and the attention tray of what waits on you. The Sessions page is in the recording at the top. `corvid-app` is a desktop app on [Uno Platform](https://platform.uno) over the same engine as `corvid chat`, on the same Corvid home. A session can be driven by one process at a time; open elsewhere, it shows read-only and follows along. - **Sessions.** The conversation with tool cards, approval cards, diffs, the queue, steering and questions, and a dock of changes. - **Board.** Every session and child at a glance, with an attention tray for what waits on you. - **Review and Rewind.** Changes since a point, with comments back to the agent; a timeline of checkpoints to restore. - **Memory, Skills, Models, Safety, Audit.** Review staged memory and consolidations, skill drafts, models and slots with downloads, approval rules and detections, and the event log with the egress ledger. - **Jobs, MCP, Gateway, Secrets, Settings.** Scheduled jobs, held MCP tools, pairing, secret names (never a value), and `corvid.json`. The app hosts the gateway and scheduler only if you turn that on (Settings › Hosting, or Start on those pages), and the status bar says so while it does. - **Keys and reach.** `Ctrl+K` opens the palette, and every area works at phone width. `corvid-app --demo` opens a scripted demo that needs no models. `corvid serve --attach` lets a window, or the browser client, attach to an engine running elsewhere. Attached mode covers Sessions and the Board's sessions; the Board's engine status and the other areas stay on the engine's machine. → [The app's README](src/Corvid.App/README.md) · [UI design](docs/plan/ui.md) ## Ways to talk to it | Command | What it is | | --- | --- | | `corvid chat` | the terminal chat: streaming, a live tool panel, inline approvals | | `corvid-app` | the [windowed app](#the-windowed-app) | | `corvid acp` | an [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com) agent on stdio for Zed, JetBrains and VS Code, with approvals as the editor's permission prompts (diff included) | | `corvid serve` | an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`/v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/models`) for Open WebUI and other front ends, loopback-only by default; `--attach` also serves windows and the browser client | | `corvid gateway` | Telegram, Discord and Slack bots with pairing codes, an owner who answers approvals, and at-least-once delivery | | `corvid mcp serve` | Corvid's memory search, skills and, optionally, project lessons offered read-only to another agent over MCP | | `corvid mcp list` · `corvid doctor` · `corvid model` · `corvid scan` · `corvid egress` · `corvid traces export` · `corvid evals` | inspection and maintenance | **Editors.** In Zed, add an `agent_servers` entry with `"command": "corvid", "args": ["acp"]`. Start it in the workspace, because a session for another directory is refused. **HTTP.** `corvid serve` listens on `http://127.0.0.1:8411`. To listen elsewhere, name a Vault secret as the bearer token (`corvid-vault set serve.token`, with a random value of at least 24 bytes). Nobody can approve a tool call over HTTP, so a call that needs approval fails the request with `approval_required`. With `Approvals: Deny`, the model answers without the tool instead. **Attached.** `corvid serve --attach` listens on a Unix socket, with `--listen ws://127.0.0.1:8737` adding a loopback port. Every connection needs a token. `corvid-app --attach
` connects, using the owner token over a socket of yours. Any other client pairs as a device: `corvid serve pair` makes a one-time code for `--pair `, and `corvid serve devices` and `corvid serve revoke ` manage them. Listening past loopback needs the owner token in Vault, and the connection has no TLS, so put it behind one. **Gateway.** Someone the configuration does not list gets a pairing code and nothing else until you approve it on this machine: `corvid gateway pair` lists codes, `corvid gateway pair approve ABCD-EFGH --owner` pairs you, and `--guest` pairs someone else, whose messages are treated as outside content. Only the owner runs commands and answers approvals. Answers are recorded in a delivery ledger in the event log, so anything unsent goes out after a restart. `corvid gateway status` shows adapters, pairings and waiting deliveries, and `corvid gateway pair tools` gives a guest their own tool allowlist. Only one process hosts the gateway at a time. → [ACP and HTTP](docs/architecture.md#acp-and-openai-compatible-http-c-019) · [Gateway](docs/architecture.md#gateway-c-020) · [Project memory over MCP](docs/architecture.md#project-memory-over-mcp-c-028) ## Configuration Configuration is read from `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/corvid/corvid.json` (section `Corvid`), from `CORVID__` environment variables, or from `--set key=value`, and it is validated at start. → [Host and CLI](docs/architecture.md#host-and-cli-c-013)
Models: local, local-server and cloud slots Remote models go under `Corvid:Models:Remote` and are named in slots like any other. A cloud key is a Vault secret (`corvid-vault set anthropic.key`, bound to the provider's host). ```json { "Corvid": { "Models": { "Remote": { "claude": { "Provider": "anthropic", "Model": "claude-opus-5-5", "Secret": "anthropic.key", "ContextWindow": 1000000, "AcceptedContext": 200000 }, "qwen-27b": { "Provider": "openai-compatible", "Endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1", "Model": "qwen3.5-27b", "ContextWindow": 32768 } }, "Slots": { "generator": { "Model": "qwen3.5-0.8b", "Escalation": ["qwen-27b", "claude"] } } }, "Privacy": { "Cloud": "Redact" } } } ``` Kev-4B is used only when configured: `--set Models:Slots:decider:Escalation:0=kev-4b`.
Subagents and model mixes ```json { "Corvid": { "Agents": { "Models": ["qwen3.5-0.8b", "qwen-27b", "claude"], "Mixes": { "reviewers": { "generator": { "Model": "qwen-27b" } } }, "Toolsets": { "reading": ["read_file", "search_files"] } } } } ``` `Models` is an optional allowlist of what a child may run: every model a mix names, and any generator, summarizer or vision model it would inherit. A child that would inherit an unlisted model is refused, so list your local generator. Empty means any catalogue model. The names must exist, so this example needs the `Models:Remote` entries above. The limits are `MaxConcurrent` (10), `MaxDepth` (1), `MaxSteps` (8), `MaxTokens` (64,000) and `MaxSeconds` (600).
Code mode, architect/editor turns and memory jobs ```json { "Corvid": { "Tools": { "Code": { "Enabled": true, "TimeoutSeconds": 300, "MaxCalls": 50 } }, "Turn": { "ArchitectEditor": true, "ImageTurns": 2 } } } ``` Code mode needs a cloud or local-server generator, and `corvid doctor` lists the Python, Node and .NET runtimes it finds. `ImageTurns` is how many of the latest messages send their images in full. Background consolidation is on by default, under `Corvid:Memory:Consolidation` ([details](docs/architecture.md#sleep-time-memory-jobs-a7)).
Kev on the GPU Use the CUDA build variant. It needs the NVIDIA driver and the CUDA 13 runtime, and `corvid doctor` checks for both. Place Kev on the GPU: ```sh corvid chat --set Models:Placement:kev-0.8b:Device=cuda --set Models:Placement:kev-0.8b:Fallback=Cpu ``` or `"Models": { "Placement": { "kev-0.8b": { "Device": "cuda", "Fallback": "Cpu" } } }` in the file. With `Fallback: Cpu`, Kev runs on the CPU, with a notice, when the GPU cannot be used. The default `Fail` leaves decisions on the degraded tier instead. Build the two variants into separate output directories ([details](docs/architecture.md#kev-on-cuda-c-029)).
MCP servers ```json { "Corvid": { "Mcp": { "Servers": { "notes": { "Command": "notes-mcp", "Arguments": ["--stdio"], "ReadOnlyPaths": ["~/notes"] }, "tracker": { "Url": "https://mcp.tracker.example/mcp", "Secret": "tracker.token", "Trust": "Trusted" } } } } } ``` Servers are untrusted by default: every tool asks before it runs, and its description and every result taint the session. `"Trust": "Trusted"` honours a server's read-only hints. Review held tools with `/mcp diff`, then take them with `/mcp accept`, or with `/mcp allow` for a flagged one, which then always asks. `"Corvid:Mcp:Serve:ProjectMemory": true` adds `get_memory` and `get_memory_context` to `corvid mcp serve`, serving approved lessons only, never local-only ones. ([details](docs/architecture.md#mcp-client-and-server-c-018))
HTTP endpoint ```json { "Corvid": { "Serve": { "Url": "http://0.0.0.0:8411", "TokenSecret": "serve.token", "Approvals": "Fail", "Tools": true } } } ```
Hosting and the egress ledger ```json { "Corvid": { "App": { "HostGateway": false, "HostScheduler": false }, "Serve": { "Attach": { "TokenSecret": "attach.owner" } }, "Privacy": { "Ledger": { "RetainDays": 90, "MaxMegabytes": 256 } } } } ``` The app starts neither the gateway nor the scheduler unless these are on or you press Start on their pages. Without `TokenSecret`, attached mode's owner token is a 0600 file in the state directory; with it, give the app the token in `CORVID_ATTACH_TOKEN` to attach as owner. `corvid egress prune` applies the ledger's limits now.
Messaging gateway ```json { "Corvid": { "Gateway": { "Adapters": { "telegram": { "Enabled": true, "Secret": "telegram.bot", "Owners": ["123456789"] }, "discord": { "Enabled": true, "Secret": "discord.bot", "Channels": ["1180000000000000000"] }, "slack": { "Enabled": true, "Secret": "slack.bot", "AppSecret": "slack.app", "HomeChat": "C0123456789", "Chats": { "C0123456789": { "Persona": "Answer briefly.", "Slots": { "generator": "claude" } } } } } } } } ``` In `vault.json`, bind each token to its API host (`api.telegram.org`, `discord.com`, `slack.com`) and toolset `gateway`. Allow `POST` as `auto`, because sends carry no approval. Telegram's token goes in the URL path, so it needs `"allowInUrl": true`. Under the default `"tainted": "ask"`, answers from a tainted session, such as a chat with a guest, are refused. Set `"tainted": "auto"` on a token only if guests should get answers.
Detection rules, scans and trace export ```sh corvid scan --fail-on high # whole log; --session for one, --json for one document corvid chat --set Detections:Enforce=false # record every match without asking corvid traces export --session --out trace.jsonl ``` `Corvid:Detections:Enforce=false` records matches without asking, so scheduled jobs never stop on a rule. `Corvid:Detections:Enabled=false` turns the inline check off. Trace export redacts secrets and cuts long strings at 4 KiB. `--retention metadata` keeps names, paths, commands and decisions but no content. Memory tool content is withheld unless `--include-local-memory` is given. `--out` writes an owner-only file and never overwrites one. `/memory import hermes [] [--dry-run]` stages Hermes memories for review, and nothing is written until you approve it.
## Status Pre-release and Linux-first. **Built:** everything above, plus calibration tooling with decision export, the golden-trajectory replay harness, the S2 tool-calling golden set and harness, spike S4's harness comparing Kev's `tool` and `done` answers with the 600-token state against a transcript-sized one ([S4](docs/spikes/S4-state-budget.md)), and a prompt-injection exfiltration canary suite. The full list is in [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md), one section per work item. How the windowed app was built, phase by phase, and what each phase left is in [`docs/plan/ui-handoff.md`](docs/plan/ui-handoff.md). **Next:** the rest of the agent plan's Phase 3 in [`docs/plan/corvid-agent.md`](docs/plan/corvid-agent.md): media memory, voice and more gateway adapters, and calibrating the decider's floors, which are not yet fitted to measured data. The terminal UI redesign in [`docs/plan/tui.md`](docs/plan/tui.md) is designed, with an inline renderer that never clears your scrollback; its mockups are in [`docs/plan/tui-mockups/`](docs/plan/tui-mockups/README.md). Today's `corvid chat` uses a simpler Spectre.Console renderer. Vault's roadmap is [`docs/plan/vault.md`](docs/plan/vault.md). ## Build and test Requires the .NET 10 SDK (10.0.401 or a later feature band). The Vault tests are Linux-only. ```sh dotnet build Corvid.slnx dotnet run --project tools/Corvid.Architecture --no-build -- . # dependency-boundary check dotnet test --solution Corvid.slnx ``` Evaluation harnesses (replay, calibration, tool-calling) are described in [`evals/README.md`](evals/README.md). ## Repository layout | Directory | Contents | | --- | --- | | `docs/plan/` | the agent plan (`corvid-agent.md`), Vault (`vault.md`), the TUI design (`tui.md`) with its mockups, the windowed UI design (`ui.md`) with its mockups, and how the app was built (`ui-handoff.md`) | | `docs/architecture.md` | how each built piece works, section by section | | `docs/spikes/`, `docs/research/` | measured spikes (S1 to S5) and the TUI research notes | | `docs/media/` | the README's recording and screenshots of the app, and how they were made | | `src/Corvid.Abstractions` | dependency-free contracts: session events, `IEventLog`, `Envelope`, `IDecider`, `IExtractor`, `ITokenCounter` | | `src/Corvid.Kernel` | event log and projections, session actors and the turn loop, compaction, durable jobs and the scheduler, checkpoints | | `src/Corvid.Fabric` | decision
